grammar.title: relative clauses
grammar.explanation: Relative clauses give extra information about a person, thing, place or time. They start with a relative pronoun: who (people), which (things), where (places), when (times) and whose (possession).
grammar.rule: who = people, which = things, where = places, when = times, whose = possession. That can replace who or which in defining relative clauses.
examples: Books about the history of flight often say it was the Wright brothers.
The whale, which was picked up by the powerful winds of Hurricane Delta, was 15 m long.
The boys, who were aged eight, ten and twelve, let the spider bite them.

values: Christopher Blair is a journalist who writes fake news.
He writes news stories which are completely fake.
This is the room where Maarten Schenk works.
He makes a note of the time when a story is first shared on social media.
This is the politician whose story went viral.

grammar.title: reported speech
grammar.explanation: When we report what someone said, we usually move the tense back one step (backshift) and change pronouns and other words.
grammar.rule: present → past: 'He is a genius' → his friends said that he was a genius. present perfect → past perfect: 'It has changed my life' → it had changed his life. will → would: 'Bali will ban single-use plastic bags' → the governor said that Bali would ban single-use plastic bags.
examples: His friends said that he was a genius.
One child in Mexico told us that it had changed his life.
The governor said that Bali would ban single-use plastic bags.

values: His friends said that he was a genius.
One child in Mexico told us that it had changed his life.
The governor said that Bali would ban single-use plastic bags.

grammar.title: will, might and be going to for predictions
grammar.explanation: We use will, might and be going to to talk about the future. Will shows strong certainty, might shows possibility, and be going to often shows a prediction based on present evidence or definite intention.
grammar.rule: will + verb = certain: 'I think print media will disappear.' might + verb = possible: 'I think it might be hard to distinguish real news from fake news.' be going to + verb = strong prediction: 'I definitely think that celebrities are going to be more prominent.'
examples: I think print media will disappear.
I think it might be hard to distinguish real news from fake news.
I definitely think that celebrities are going to be more prominent.
We will bring you wonderful stories from all around the world.
We probably won’t publish stories about disasters.

values: I think print media will disappear.
I think it might be hard to distinguish real news from fake news.
I definitely think that celebrities are going to be more prominent.

grammar.title: used to
grammar.explanation: We use used to + verb to talk about a regular habit or a state in the past that is no longer true.
grammar.rule: used to + infinitive for habits and states in the past: 'He used to draw at school.' Didn't use to + infinitive for negatives: 'I didn't use to like vegetables.' Compare with a single past event: 'He painted his first painting when he was seven.'
examples: He used to arrive at his studio in the afternoon.
He used to pay his bills by giving people drawings instead of money.
I used to collect toy cars when I was a child.
We used to live in the countryside.

values: He used to listen to his father playing the piano.
I didn't use to like playing sports at school.
He immediately fell in love with the instrument.

grammar.title: comparatives and superlatives
grammar.explanation: We use comparatives to compare two things and superlatives to say something is the best, biggest, most important, etc.
grammar.rule: Short adjectives/adverbs: add -er/-est (hard, harder, the hardest). Longer adjectives or -ly adverbs: use more / the most (more carefully, the most important). Irregular: good/well - better - the best; far - further/farther - the furthest/farthest. We can also use (not) as + adjective + as to make comparisons.
examples: Creativity is the most important part of my job.
I think being creative is just as important as these other things.
I think it makes my films more interesting.
It’s easier for me to get ideas when I’m outside.
It’s the hardest thing about cooking.

values: I have to work harder when I’m at home.
the most important part of my job
That's the best thing about cooking.
Creativity is just as important as these other things.

grammar.title: present perfect + for, since and yet
grammar.explanation: We use the present perfect with for, since and yet to talk about something that started in the past and is still true now.
grammar.rule: for = a period of time (for more than ten years). since = a particular time in the past (since the start of his career). yet = ‘at any time up to now’, used with negatives to emphasise that something hasn’t happened but we expect it to happen soon.
examples: The art gallery has supported Yinka since the start of his career.
Nigel Schofield has worked with Yinka for more than ten years.
Yinka hasn't seen the finished sculpture yet.

values: Nigel Schofield has worked with Yinka for more than ten years.
a particular time in the past
The art gallery has supported Yinka since the start of his career.
negative: not happened up to now
Yinka hasn't seen the finished sculpture yet.

grammar.title: first and second conditionals
grammar.explanation: The first conditional describes a real, possible situation in the future. The second conditional describes a hypothetical or imaginary situation.
grammar.rule: First conditional: If + present simple + will (If you travel to somewhere new, you'll understand the culture better.) Second conditional: If + past simple + would (If everyone took their litter home with them, tourist destinations would be a lot cleaner.)
examples: If you travel to somewhere new, you'll understand the culture better if you read a book about its history.
If you try to speak their language, people will appreciate your efforts.
If people tried going somewhere different, the main tourist destinations wouldn't be so busy.
If everyone took their litter home with them, tourist destinations would be a lot cleaner and more attractive.

values: If you try to speak their language, people will appreciate your efforts.
If people tried going somewhere different, the main tourist destinations wouldn't be so busy.

grammar.title: reflexive pronouns
grammar.explanation: We use reflexive pronouns (myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves) when the object of a verb is the same person as the subject. The phrase by myself/yourself… means "alone".
grammar.rule: myself / yourself / himself / herself / itself / ourselves / yourselves / themselves. By + reflexive pronoun = alone: "Do you prefer travelling by yourself?"
examples: Do you prefer travelling by yourself?
I like the freedom of travelling by myself.
My brother likes travelling by himself.
Ana prefers walking by herself.
You always go by yourself.

values: I like the freedom of travelling by myself.
Do you prefer travelling by yourself?
My brother likes travelling by himself.

grammar.title: can, could, be able to
grammar.explanation: We use can / can’t for ability in the present, and could / couldn’t for general ability in the past. Be able to is used for all tenses and for specific past achievements.
grammar.rule: Present: can / can't / am able to. Past: could / couldn't for general ability; was/were able to for specific successful actions. Be able to works with other tenses: 'I'm able to install a washing machine.'
examples: I could draw quite well.
I was able to use my skills to design clothes.
I can fix a roof.
I'm able to install a washing machine.
I can't play video games.
I couldn't do any of that a few years ago.

values: I can fix a roof. I can't play video games.
I could draw quite well. I couldn’t do any of that a few years ago.
I was able to use my skills to design clothes.
I'm able to install a washing machine.

grammar.title: active and passive
grammar.explanation: In the active voice, the subject does the action: "People share the videos." In the passive voice, the important information is the action or the thing affected, not who did it.
grammar.rule: Passive: be + past participle. Present: is/are + past participle ("Hundreds of hours of video are uploaded."). Past: was/were + past participle ("Journalists were sent somewhere to report."). We use the passive when it ’s not important or not known who does or did the action.
examples: Every minute, hundreds of hours of video are uploaded to YouTube.
Every year, more and more videos are shared online.
In the past, journalists were sent somewhere to report on a news event.
When students watch these videos, they feel more motivated.

values: These kinds of videos are watched every day.
People shared the video more than 6 million times.
The video was shared more than 6 million times.
The teachers give the students homework.
The students are given homework every day.
Jenna uploaded the clip to YouTube.
The clip was uploaded to YouTube.

grammar.title: How to... describe a problem and make recommendations
grammar.explanation: To describe a problem: There’s a problem with... / The ... isn’t working. / I can’t ... / It won’t ... / It keeps (crashing). / When/Every time I ... , it ... / I think it’s (broken).
grammar.rule: To make recommendations: Have you tried + -ing ...? / Try + -ing ... / Have you checked ...? / Maybe you could ... + verb. To respond: Yes, I’ll try that. / Yes, that works. / Yes, it’s working now.
examples: There's a problem with my internet connection.
The printer isn’t working.
It keeps crashing when I open the file.
Have you tried restarting it?
Maybe you could check the wifi.

grammar.title: -ing form
grammar.explanation: Some verbs are followed by the -ing form of another verb: I started learning them. She spends an hour every week talking to different people.
grammar.rule: Verbs followed by -ing: enjoy, hate, imagine, like, love, practise, recommend, remember, spend time, start, stop, suggest, try, etc. Example: I like learning languages.
examples: I started learning them.
She spends an hour every week talking to different people.
I like learning languages.
I can't stand translating!
I recommend going to a class.

values: She spends an hour every week talking to different people.
Personally, I enjoy studying with other people more than by myself.
I recommend going to a class.
I remember listening to my favourite British bands years ago.
